source.title: SEUF: Is Unlearning One Expert Enough for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs?
source.authors: Hao-Min Zhuang; Yihua Zhang; Ke-Han Guo; Jing-Han Jia; Gaowen Liu; Si-Jia Liu; Xiangliang Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests unlearning on MoE models and reports that existing methods can cause poor utility and expert-selection shifts; it also proposes and evaluates a method intended to address these limitations.
record.gate_note: The reported unlearning metrics and the GCG attack are study results. Table 1's parameter-configuration comparison, the remaining RWKU methods and PEFT/random-selection comparisons, and additional expert-affinity comparisons are not included as rows; they are not needed to represent the tested claim versions within the row limit.
record.test_reason: The study applies GA, GDiff, NPO and RMU to two MoE LLMs on WMDP-Cyber and RWKU and reports forget accuracy and MMLU utility (Table 3). Its expert-selection analysis (Fig. 3) argues that standard methods give 'fake unlearning': routers bypass the target experts, leaving them out of reach. It also proposes SEUF and tests it against a GCG jailbreak. Together these bear on A, C, E and F.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that standard unlearning on MoE LLMs causes expert-selection shifts. Routers bypass the target experts, which they call shortcut or 'fake' unlearning, and utility drops sharply. SEUF unlearns only the top-1 affinity expert and adds a router anchor loss. They report up to 5% better forgetting and 35% better utility while updating 0.06% of parameters, and say GCG fails to recover forgotten knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: Applies existing unlearning methods to MoE models and introduces SEUF, which selects target experts and anchors routing; it is not a reproduction of the listed original-source studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by MoE model, benchmark, unlearning method, and whether SEUF is used. Expert selection also changes over unlearning iterations.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper states that all experiments were conducted in a single run without multiple trials. Evaluation covers two benchmarks, and the GCG attack is reported for one model and one SEUF+GA setting. The expert-overlap and forget-loss results are figure-only in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: Table 1's additional GA tunable-module configurations; Table 3's GD IFF, NPO, PEFT, random-selection and remaining RWKU method results; Table 5's layer-wise expert-affinity/utility values; Appendix sensitivity, sampling-overlap, and Mixtral results. Prioritized the core WMDP method comparisons, selected RWKU comparisons, mechanism analysis, and GCG result.

untested.parts: No activation-direction ablation, and no attempt to recover knowledge by re-routing to the bypassed target experts.
Only GCG was tried, and only on SEUF+GA/DeepSeek/RWKU. No rephrasing, other languages or in-context attacks. No attack on models unlearned by the standard methods without SEUF.
SEUF was tested only against GCG. It was not tested against fine-tuning, ablation, quantization or other prompting attacks.
Robustness to relearning, quantization and internal-edit attacks was not tested.

missing.what: Comparison of MoE versus dense LLMs (Phi3.5, LLaMA3-8B) under the same four methods. MoE points cluster at worse forget and utility drops, which bears on where A holds.
Under GCG, the target expert's affinity score falls but the expert stays ranked top-1. This is the mechanism behind the robustness claim.
Mixtral 8x7B SEUF results: WMDP FE 0.2608 / UT 0.6364; RWKU FE 0.0455 / UT 0.6713 (pretrained UT 0.6885). Declared as left out, but relevant to A for a larger model.

record.verdict_notes: All results come from single runs. Checkpoints were chosen for the best FE/UT balance, which flatters every method. The 'blocks access' interpretation for C rests only on routing overlap, not on recovered knowledge. The GCG test covers one model, one method and one benchmark.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt attacks other than GCG recover knowledge. Utility is measured with MMLU, and targeted knowledge with WMDP-Cyber or RWKU.
No post-unlearning relearning or fine-tuning attack is tested.
No activation direction is ablated. The study analyzes expert-selection shifts and interprets them as leaving target experts out of reach.
Only the GCG white-box prompt attack on DeepSeek unlearned by SEUF+GA is tested; rephrasing, other languages, in-context information, and other jailbreaks are not tested.
SEUF is tested against GCG only, not against fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or the other prompting attacks named in the claim.

relationships.condition: Standard GA/GDiff/NPO/RMU without SEUF on Qwen1.5-MoE and DeepSeek-V2-Lite
relationships.reason: Forgetting sometimes reaches near chance or zero (r5, r25, r29, r33, r41, r45). Utility often collapses, e.g. Qwen MMLU 0.598→0.24–0.36 (r2, r6, r10, r26, r42), and several FE values stay well above chance (r17, r21).
relationships.display_finding: Standard methods sometimes reached chance or zero target accuracy, but Qwen MMLU fell from 0.598 to 0.24–0.36 and several settings retained above-chance knowledge.

tranche.reason: The Sec. 3 pilot (Table 1, Fig. 1a) and Insight 2 give results and a specific argument that standard unlearning on MoE LLMs fails to keep utility and is 'fake' through routing shortcuts. That says version A needs restating for MoE, which is T5. T5 ranks ahead of T3 in the rules.

source_check.notes: Table 3 matches the verdict rows: r1-r32 are WMDP (method x model, without then with SEUF, FE then UT); r33-r48 are RWKU for GA and RMU only, so GDiff and NPO RWKU are not in rows. All experiments are single runs (App. A). The GCG result covers one model, with FE taken only on outputs containing 'answer'. Fig. 3 names no model (DeepSeek by context).

statements.correction: 2411.18797: GA on WMDP. MoE model (DeepSeek-V2-Lite by context, 16B total). Expert-selection overlap with the pretrained model declines steadily over unlearning (Fig. 3a, figure only) while forget loss falls (Fig. 3b). The authors infer that routers bypass the target experts ('fake unlearning'; target experts 'remain hidden out of the reach'). No similarity metric or recovery attack was run.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers for this study but cites r50 under 'representations and weight traces stay close to the original'. r50 measures expert-selection overlap with the pretrained model, and that overlap declines. No weight or representation similarity is measured. The study is a 16B MoE, outside the stated 3B-7B and outside the Jaccard/CKA/PCA/access metrics. It fits C's 'blocks access rather than deleting' clause only by the authors' inference.

statements.correction: Optional addition: 2411.18797 (SEUF+GA, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, RWKU): white-box GCG with 5,000 steps, 400 prompts over 400 samples; FE (Rouge-L recall) 0.01 before and after; FE taken only on outputs containing 'answer'.
statements.problem: The study is cited via r49 but not named. What the statement implies for it is right: SEUF is the authors' own method, they attacked it with white-box GCG, and nothing was recovered. RWKU in the conditions fits. Caveats a reader would want: FE was computed only on outputs containing 'answer'; one model, one run.
